other.about: SSE4's shipped class atlas (C2): physical type, surface state, gas mix and pressure, human habitability profiles, and every star and remnant's class. Generated by scripts/build-base-atlas.py.

schemes.question: What kind of object is this?
What is its air made of, and how much is there?
What do people need to live here?
What kind of star is this?

axes.label: star family (from temperature, gravity and phase)

learn.summary: Too small to pull itself round: an asteroid, comet or small moon.
Dark, carbon-rich and primitive (C-type), like Bennu.
A dirty snowball: a comet or an icy small body, like 67P.
Mostly iron and nickel (M-type), perhaps a stripped core, like 16 Psyche.
Silicate rock with some metal (S-type), like Eros.
A world with an outsized iron core, like Mercury.
Rock around an iron core: Earth, Venus, Mars, the Moon, Io.
Rock and a deep layer of water or ice: Ganymede, Titan, Pluto, perhaps some exoplanets.
Rock and ice under a thick hydrogen envelope; the commonest planets in the galaxy and absent from ours.
Mostly water, ammonia and methane ices under a hydrogen-helium sky: Uranus, Neptune.
Mostly hydrogen and helium: Jupiter, Saturn.
Cold enough for ammonia clouds: Jupiter and Saturn (Sudarsky class I).
Warm enough that water clouds form instead (class II).
Too warm for water clouds, too cool for metal ones: clear blue skies (class III).
Hot: sodium and potassium dominate the colours (class IV).
Very hot: clouds of rock vapour (class V).
So hot that molecules break apart on the day side.
Above about 13 Jupiter masses: deuterium burns for a while. A failed star, not a planet.
One face always to its star: a day side and a night side.
A strongly oval orbit: seasons set by distance.
Has a ring system.
Strongly volcanic, with lava or with ice.
Heated from inside by tides.
No magnetic field of its own to keep the stellar wind off.
Less than about 100 million years old.
Older than about 10 billion years.

examples.name: illustrative: an Earth-like world 11 billion years old

learn.summary: Drifts between the stars with no star of its own.
Captured rather than formed where it is.
Has a biosphere.
People live here.
Made habitable by deliberate engineering.
A loose pile of rubble held by its own weak gravity.
Two bodies that met gently and stayed together.
A giant blown up far larger than its mass suggests.
A super-Jupiter, close to the brown-dwarf limit.
Bare rock or regolith under a black sky: the Moon, Mercury.
A surface of lava.
A crushing, scorching air trapping its heat: Venus.
Hot, dry and open to the sky.

learn.summary: Mild temperatures but little open water.

examples.name: illustrative: Earth with its oceans gone

learn.summary: Seas and land under a mild sky: Earth.
Water from pole to pole.
Cold, dry, thin-aired: Mars.
Ice-covered except for a band of open water or bare ground at the equator.
Frozen solid from pole to pole: Pluto, Triton.
An ice shell over a hidden ocean: Europa, Enceladus, Ganymede.
Lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane: Titan.
A global ocean under a hydrogen sky: proposed, not yet confirmed.
No air to speak of.
Nitrogen with free oxygen: Earth's mix.
Nitrogen without free oxygen: Titan, Triton, Pluto.
Carbon dioxide: Venus, Mars.
The primordial mix of the giants.
Sulphur compounds: Io's thin air.
Mostly water vapour: a steam world.
Mostly methane.
Too little to feel.
A wisp: Mars.
Thin: a mountaintop and above.

examples.name: illustrative: a high-plateau world with thin oxygen

learn.summary: About Earth's sea level.
Dense.
Very dense.
Crushing: Venus, or deep in a giant.
Breathable oxygen but enough carbon dioxide to need a filter mask.
People can live here only inside a sealed, shielded habitat.
A pressure suit lets people work outside.
Warm clothes and bottled air are enough.
